<reason>Side B (PRO) opened with a vivid, plausible anchor — interest now exceeding defense — plus sequencing, credibility, and intergenerational fairness. But Side A (CON) located and relentlessly exploited the decisive vulnerability: B's own characterization of the plan as "a pause on addition, not a program of subtraction," combined with B's honest admission that no ten-year savings figure exists. A converted that into a clean decision rule ("risk aversion is only a reason to act if the action reduces the risk") and showed that the interest line B built its case on is driven by existing stock, rates, and aging programs the rule leaves untouched. A further squeezed B's concessions — exempting self-financing investment, binding tax cuts, placing the burden on each proponent — into the charge that PRO had described ordinary case-by-case budgeting, which is precisely what the motion's blanket priority rule forbids. B's replies (accretion of "just one more program," and the certainty asymmetry between a current interest line item and speculative future returns) were genuinely good and kept the debate competitive, and B's pressure questions forced A to supply both a vetting mechanism and a threshold, which A answered directly and in format. But B's closing leaned on "ordinary budgeting got us here" without ever repairing the core targeting/no-savings problem, so A's route to victory survived intact. A's clipped opening is a real execution cost, but the lost material was marginal.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's exploitation of [B2.4]: turning PRO's own "pause on addition, not subtraction" framing plus the conceded absence of any savings figure into the claim that the rule forgoes real capacity to buy a deficit reduction of roughly zero — a targeting failure B never squarely repaired.</best_rebuttal>
